entries.title: Steve Scalise Takes His House Defense to the Red Dots of the Northeast
entries.summary: The majority leader hopes to defend his majority — and perhaps his job.
entries.content:
PORTSMOUTH, New Hampshire — Nancy Pelosi got one thing right in 2018 that the current House minority leader hasn’t, Majority Leader Steve Scalise said during a barnstorming trip across the Northeast last week.

Democrats that year won a blowout midterm election, making Pelosi the speaker. Her edge, which is missing this year, the Louisiana Republican said, was quality candidates.

Those belong to the GOP, he argued. And even in a bluer part of the country in a year when many expect a 2018 redux, Scalise said his party has superior contenders who can buoy Republicans regardless of the political climate.

“They're defending socialism right now, which is a whole different problem for Democrats that we're using in our contrast,” Scalise told the Washington Sun at a fundraising stop amid a campaign swing to boost six races in four states.

Scalise knows there are enormous challenges to overcome, with the Iran war and tariffs driving up prices for food, goods and fuel, all tied to a Republican president who is submarining in the polls

And yet, Scalise said, in a wide-ranging interview those things are on the mend.

“If you look at something like gas prices, which were coming down before Iran, and when Iran is resolved, number one, Iran won't have a nuclear weapon which is good for all of us. But also, gas prices will come down even lower,” he said.

The biggest issue facing Republicans in this election really is “making sure people get out and vote,” he said.

That’s where the candidates come in.

Scalise’s first stop was Portsmouth, promoting Anthony DiLorenzo in the race to replace Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas, who’s running for Senate in New Hampshire, and to boost Paul LePage, the former governor of Maine now seeking to replace outgoing Democratic Rep. Jared Golden, just across the border..

Scalise pointed to LePage, “one of the superstars of the recruiting cycle,” as exhibit A for quality. The Mainer is widely expected to win the seat, with Cook Political Report rating his contest as “Likely Republican.”

DiLorenzo, a wealthy car dealer, faces more of an uphill slog in a district rated “Likely Democrat,” but Scalise professed optimism.

“I think you go back a few months ago, this seat wasn't as high on most people's radar as the Maine seat, but it's become that way because of the strength of our candidate,” Scalise said. “So, you know, having really good candidates allows us to compete in districts like this. If you have an average candidate, you're not going to be competitive. We've got great candidates.”

In New York’s Hudson Valley a day later, Scalise tried to turn the 2026 keystone argument about affordability in favor of Rep. Mike Lawler, who helped raise the federal tax-exemption cap on state and local taxes in last year’s reconciliation bill.

Standing alongside Lawler in a local diner, Scalise said he’d brought a “trophy” for Lawler, picking up a salt shaker off a table and handing it to him.

“The king of SALT,” Scalise proclaimed to the crowd, using the acronym for the tax break that heavily impacts Lawler’s constituents. “I'd be somewhere, and next thing you know I got like four salt shakers showing up on my table before the bill passed, and I knew Lawler was in the restaurant.”

This two-day stretch in three states is just a fraction of the travel the Louisianan is doing this election cycle. After the first stop in Portsmouth, he pulled out his phone to show a picture of a shirt he had his staff create. On the back was a map of the country with a star on every district he’s traveled to or plans to travel to leading up to Nov. 3.

“It’s like a rock band tour,” Scalise said. “We’ve been in I think 34 districts just during August recess, way more than that during this period, and that's what it's going to take. You got to leave it all out on the field.”

This travel is nothing new for Scalise, who ascended to Republican leadership in 2014 when he won a race for Republican whip. Every election year, vulnerable Republicans and new candidates have come to expect Scalise will stump for them.

It’s part of what’s garnered him loyalty among members of the Republican Conference, to the point that he’s never faced any serious challenges to his position as he rose through the ranks.

There’s a parallel contest going on as he tries to defend the party’s control of Congress; it may also help him defend his place in leadership.

House Judiciary Chairman Jim Jordan of Ohio has been laying the groundwork to challenge Scalise should Republicans lose, The Washington Sun has previously reported. Jordan has also been hitting the road for candidates and incumbents this cycle, something that’s caught the eye of many Republicans.

Scalise acknowledged he could face a challenge but said he remained focused on keeping, and potentially growing, the Republican majority.

“Look, it's a free country. Anybody can run, and none of these positions are guaranteed,” Scalise said, though he also laid out a case for himself.

“I have a great working relationship with President Trump and his staff, and because of that, we've been able to get some of the most consequential things done with the smallest majority we've ever had. That doesn't happen by accident,” Scalise said. “Anybody else can run, so you know that's always going to be something that you deal with after the election. But I'm not concerned about it right now.”

Pressed on whether he’s confident he can beat back any potential challenge from Jordan, Scalise reiterated that all his focus is on winning in November, but he added a subtle warning shot.

“The only way we do that is if every ounce of our energy is focused on that, and not all these people that are hoping that we lose so that they can run for other seats,” he said.

entries.title: Advocates Hold Another Rally in Support of East Potomac Park
entries.summary: Ex-Olympian David Hearn, who had been accused of vandalizing the reflecting pool in June, joined dozens of protesters at the rally.
entries.content:
Gloomy weather was no deterrent for dozens of protesters who made their way to East Potomac Park on Sunday morning for Hains Point Hoopla 3.0 — the third iteration of the Washington Area Bicyclist’s Association's efforts to draw attention to the uncertain future of the national park.

Ex-Olympian David Hearn, whom the Trump administration had accused of vandalizing the reflecting pool in June and whose federal case was dismissed with prejudice on Thursday, joined local advocates at the rally.

“I'm proud to be here today as a free man,” he told the crowd. “It was a difficult 104 days being accused by the top leadership of our country of being guilty of something I didn't do and having a contrived set of charges against me.”

The protest underscored the fears that some locals have about the administration’s intention to transform the East Potomac Golf Links into a luxury golf course that will be inaccessible to many members of the public, in a renovation that could eliminate other recreational uses of the park.

Rebecca Miller, the executive director of the D.C. Preservation League, said the fight for the park is becoming urgent. The recently introduced Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act includes a section that she believes will “gut”Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act, which allows non-federal actors to intervene if there is the potential harm to historic sites and has formed the basis of the group’s lawsuit opposing the East Potomac renovation.

“That law is what is protecting this site currently,” she said. “That is what we are suing under on all of these different actions.”

The Maryland-born Hearn, who was arrested less than four miles from Hains Point, called the park “an invaluable resource for the public,” adding that “through all the trials and tribulations for me over the past four months, I was able to ride my bike [there] every day. I know for a lot of people coming out here is a great way to relieve stress as well.”

Local resident Marc Blackman, who called the park “an oasis in the desert,” said he wanted the park to remain open to the public as it has for more than a century. He added that he views the Trump administration’s efforts in East Potomac and elsewhere around the D.C. area as a “total disregard of the Washington metropolitan area and all the other presumptive beautification projects that are going on, all of which sully rather than beautify the space.”

Peter Harnick, the founder of the Rails-to-Trails Conservancy, expressed similar frustrations.

“It's been terrible,” he said. “They're not telling us what they want to do. They're not telling us how they're going to go about doing it. Zero transparency. And this is our park.”

At-Large D.C. Council member Robert White, who attended the rally for the second time, told The Washington Sun in an interview that his late mother used to bring him to the park when he was a child. As a college student, White learned to play golf with his brother on the golf course.

“He ended up locked up for a number of years,” White said of his brother. “I was coming out here by myself, missing my brother. So this place is very special to me in different parts of my life.”

Throughout the rally, speakers denounced the potential removal of bike lanes, fields and trees from the park. But less than a mile away, the sound of saws reverberated across the golf course as a crew of National Park Service arborists appeared to be in the process of clearing several trees from a mature grove.

In a statement, a spokesperson for the Interior Department said the tree removals were part of routine maintenance “with selective removal of hazard trees, non-native invasive trees and declining and dying trees that cannot be brought back to good health through any degree of intervention.”

As protesters dispersed from the rally, very few seemed to notice the tree removal crew.

entries.title: All-DMV High School Football Players of Week 6
entries.summary: This weekend’s standouts include a do-it-all athlete from Paint Branch and an efficient quarterback from Bullis.
entries.content:
This story is part of The Washington Sun’s All-DMV coverage. All-DMV is a new collaboration between The Sun, Fox5 DC, NBC4 Washington and WTOP News, aimed at covering the D.C. area’s best high school athletes. Every week, we’ll have a volleyball players of the week story on Wednesday, and boys and girls soccer selections Friday. You can find past players of the week and more information about All-DMV here. 

While Week 6 of the high school football season in the DMV was complicated by inclement weather, these standout athletes still found a way to shine despite the rain. Here’s who earned Washington Sun Player of the Week honors this week:

Alijah Bah, Senior, Athlete, Paint Branch

Paint Branch coach Mike Nesmith likes to call Bah an “old-school” high school football player. He’s the Panthers’ bellcow running back on offense and doubles as a dangerous defensive back on defense. He also returns kicks and punts — Bah rarely gets a play off on Friday nights.

Friday against Bethesda-Chevy Chase, Bah was everywhere. He totaled 184 scrimmage yards and two touchdowns on offense, including the go-ahead score in an eventual 15-8 win. He also nabbed two interceptions on defense and recovered the game-sealing fumble late in the fourth quarter.

“He truly is one of the best players I’ve ever had the privilege of coaching, and a great competitor,” Nesmith said. “He’s really coming into his own as a leader, and I just couldn’t be more proud of him and his development.”

Darius Knight, Senior, Running Back, Dunbar

Last season, Knight was one of several explosive running backs that shared a talented Dunbar backfield. After several teammates graduated, he’s now the go-to ball carrier for the Crimson Tide. Thursday against Bell, Knight carried the ball 18 times for 205 yards and four touchdowns in a 40-16 win. Knight has eclipsed the 100-yard mark in each of his starts this season.

“Everybody’s going to game plan for him,” Coach Maurice Vaughn said. “I’m glad he’s got red and black on.”

Braden Nyce, Junior, Quarterback, Bullis

The Bulldogs rebounded from last week’s 11-point loss to Loyola Blakefield with a dominant showing against DCIAA contender Theodore Roosevelt. Nyce scored four touchdowns — three through the air and one on the ground — in just the first half of an eventual 40-6 win.

Two of his touchdown throws were delivered to standout wide receiver Kaleb McGhee Rivero, one of several playmakers in an explosive Bullis offense.

Theo Riley, Senior, Athlete, Wise

Riley excelled in all three phases for Wise, which blew out DuVal 71-6 Friday to move to 4-0. The senior ran for 92 yards and a touchdown on offense at running back and registered a sack at linebacker on defense. He also ran back a kickoff 64 yards for a second score on special teams.

Coach Steve Rapp’s team, always a Prince George’s County heavyweight, is averaging 50 points per game on offense through the first month of the season.

Jamal Sullivan, Senior, Athlete, Washington-Liberty

Under coach Josh Shapiro, Washington-Liberty typically runs a pass-happy “air-raid” offense. But due to rainy conditions Friday night in Virginia, the Generals needed to pivot to the run game against local rival Wakefield. Shapiro turned to Sullivan, who rewarded his coach’s trust with 113 scrimmage yards and three touchdowns as Washington-Liberty earned a 30-0 shutout victory.

The highlight of Sullivan’s night came in the first half when he streaked up the sideline for an 88-yard score to give his team an early advantage they wouldn’t look back from.

entries.title: The Washington Sun Metro: Beauty Is Pain
entries.content:
Good morning. This is The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for Oct. 5, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

In today’s newsletter: Another rally to save East Potomac, the Commanders in London and funding for Black neighborhood preservation in D.C.

Capital Weather’s Daily Digit — 7/10: After morning clouds burn off, a “sun”-sational 70-degree afternoon. Full forecast from Capital Weather.

THE LATEST

D.C. residents rallied again Sunday at East Potomac Park over fears that it will be transformed into an inaccessible luxury golf course, The Washington Sun's Shamira Muhammad reports.

But less than a mile away, the sound of saws reverberated across the golf course as a crew of National Park Service arborists appeared to be in the process of clearing several trees from a mature grove.

It goes to show how urgent the fight for the park is becoming, said Rebecca Miller, the executive director of the D.C. Preservation League. The recently introduced Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act includes a section that she believes will “gut” Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act, which allows non-federal actors to intervene if there is the potential harm to historic sites and has formed the basis of the group’s lawsuit opposing the East Potomac renovation.

“That law is what is protecting this site currently,” Miller said. “That is what we are suing under on all of these different actions.”

The rally also laid bare the different way D.C. locals see “beauty” as compared to President Donald Trump, whose beautification projects around the District include the park, freshly gilded monuments, a triumphal arch — “All of which sully rather than beautify the space,” local resident Marc Blackman told The Sun.





FROM THE DISTRICT

Could D.C.’s next mayor get a pay bump? A new bill introduced by At-Large council member Anita Bonds would push the chief executive’s pay to $290,000 next year, up from the $250,000 that Mayor Muriel Bowser has been bringing in annually since 2023. Bowser is already among the highest-paid mayors in the country, and if the raise passes council muster, her likely successor Janeese Lewis George would only slightly trail New York’s Zohran Mamdani. Now, to be fair, D.C. doesn’t have its own version of Gracie Mansion; our mayor has always paid their own rent or mortgage.

“We need finality. We need either an acquittal or a conviction,” said D.C. Council Chair Phil Mendelson on WAMU 88.5’s “The Politics Hour” on Friday, weighing in on what will be U.S. Attorney for D.C. Jeanine Pirro’s decision on whether to retry Ward 8 council member Trayon White on bribery charges after a mistrial. Her verdict is expected later this month; if she chooses against another trial, White will still face political and personal challenges.

The National Park Service has awarded D.C. a $72,000 grant for Black neighborhood preservation, The Sun’s Justice Covert reports. The D.C. Office of Planning can spend the funds on a new nomination to the National Register of Historic Places.

This year's Kennedy Center Honors will be held at the Capital One arena in downtown D.C., rather than at the storied venue itself, FOX5 DC reports.

Transit nerds rejoice. Metro is scrapping plans to get rid of the iconic color stripe design on top of pylons marking train station entrances after weeks of fierce customer pushback, The Sun’s Kendall Staton reports.

Richard Ables Sr. saw generations of Black Washingtonians through the process of burying a loved one at Hall Brothers Funeral Home, until the D.C. fixture closed seven years ago. Ables, who died last month, planned his own send-off, too, The Washington Post reports.





FROM VIRGINIA

At last week’s annual Mid-Atlantic Police Motorcycle Rodeo, motor officers navigated orange cone-lined courses at Dulles Town Center to show off their skills and train for the job, The Washington Post reports.





TRIVIA


Maryland is one of only 4 states in the country with a law mandating the youngest age a child can be left home alone. What is the minimum age?

  1. 8 years old
  2. 10 years old
  3. 14 years old
Email us the answer — the first reader who gets it right gets a shout out. The answer will be at the end of the newsletter tomorrow.





SPORTS

The Commanders’ season hit another setback on Sunday, as backup quarterback Marcus Mariota — starting in relief of the injured Jayden Daniels — was knocked out in the first quarter of their 30-13 loss to the Colts in London, reports The Sun’s Martenzie Johnson from historic Tottenham Hotspur Stadium. The Washington fans who made the trip across the Atlantic instead were left to watch third-string rookie Athan Kaliakmanis — who, to be fair, held up better than one might expect from a seventh-round draft pick — in a less-than-stellar QB duel with the Colts’ Daniel Jones. (So much for trying to convert the British into American football fans.)

Now 1-3, the Commanders desperately need Daniels to return for next Sunday’s game against the Giants, writes The Sun’s Dave Sheinin.

In the hours after their playoff exit Wednesday, the Mystics decided to keep the night going. In a fun story wrapping up Washington’s breakthrough season, The Sun’s Emma Baccellieri details the late-night “cute little kumbaya” the tight-knit group of players held at guard Georgia Amoore’s apartment before they all dispersed for the offseason.





Thank you for reading! If you liked this newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@washsun.com.

The newsletter was produced by Jeff Dooley, Jaden Amos and Gaby Morera Di Núbila.

entries.title: Morning Sun: The Final Countdown
entries.content:
Today’s notice: Millions are pouring in but what kind of campaign money matters? Road-tripping with Scalise. Truth telling from red-state Republicans. The down-ballot play. Inside SCOTUS’ Red Mass. And: Officials are still bracing for some Election Day turbulence.





THE LATEST

Welcome to Sprint Week. As the general election hits its most fevered pitch for the next month, we’re going to explore the outstanding questions that will define the next few weeks and that won’t be answered until the votes are counted, canvassed and possibly litigated. First up: Will Republican money change the story of this election? 

“We do see this level of spending actually moving numbers in our races and our internal polling,” one national GOP strategist told The Washington Sun’s Manuela Silva last week. The Republican midterm moneybomb is basically unchecked all over the map: Senate Democrats recently added $2 million in Texas spending after their Republican counterparts dropped $130 million. And that number is just part of the GOP money flow in Texas.

“We have put together an operation that’s forced Republicans to spend $220 million in what should be one of their strongholds,” Texas Democratic Party Chair Kendall Scudder told us. “So Texas Democrats are putting up a real fight here, Republicans know it, that’s why they’re spending money.”

In theory, the spending disparity can do a lot. The national GOP strategist Manuela spoke to said that money does not just buy TV ads — it can fund organizing and GOTV operations, the high-cost programs aimed at pulling out the low-propensity voters motivated by support for Donald Trump who Republicans have told us all year are key to their strategy.

But, the money flow can send signals, too. National Democratic-allied groups told The Sun earlier this year they were finding it very difficult to to fundraise — leadership faceplants inside party orgs like the DNC and the divisive primaries have made giving to “the Democrats” unappealing. But giving to specific Democrats is a different story.

“Our candidates are outraising their Republicans hand-over-fist,” a Democratic strategist familiar with House races told Manuela. On Friday, the Democrats’ House campaign arm touted huge fundraising hauls from several of their battleground candidates.

The candidate-level disparity has also been true in Senate races at times this year — Democratic candidates are raising more than their opponents, while Republicans have more outside money helping them than Democratic candidates do. This month could see that story change though — one super PAC backing Democratic Senate candidates said in a recent memo they expect to continue being outspent by Republicans, but also that they expect the amount they’re outspent by to shrink significantly in October — maybe even reaching parity in some places.

In sum, the money question is a little more complicated than who can buy the most ads. Republicans have proven very capable of raising big money to help the GOP broadly. While Democrats have seen their candidates excite donors on a race-by-race level. Which money is the more important money? We won’t know until this election is over with.

  • Sam Altman: ‘The world should accept some bad things happening’ for the benefits of AI (Politico)
  • Poll: Latino voters swing away from Trump and Republicans (NBC)




FROM THE CAMPAIGN TRAIL


On the road with Steve Scalise. “We’ve been in, I think, 34 districts just during August recess, way more than that during this period, and that's what it's going to take,” the House majority leader told The Sun’s Reese Gorman. “You got to leave it all out on the field.”

Reese tagged along with Scalise in stops in New Hampshire and New York, describing a pro in his element. Scalise told him the final push is about contrast with Democrats (“They're defending socialism right now”) and painting a rosy picture of the political moment: “If you look at something like gas prices, which were coming down before Iran, and when Iran is resolved, number one, Iran won't have a nuclear weapon which is good for all of us. But also, gas prices will come down even lower,” he said.

Red state GOP senators are increasingly saying something very different, The Sun’s Avani Kalra reports. We screwed up is the take from Republicans in safe red states or not on the ballot right now. Republicans, not just the president, have made missteps while speaking with Americans about the economy, Sen. Jim Justice (R-West Virginia) said.

“I'm not going to tell the voters, ‘Oh, it's President Biden’s fault, and it's not that bad, you shouldn’t believe your checkbooks,’” said Sen. John Kennedy (R-Louisiana). He added: “I also tell them the truth: The main reason for the resurgence in inflation is the Iran War. I think they appreciate the truth, but they’re angry.”



The Senate GOP’s gubernatorial bailout? One of the reasons Republican-allied outside groups continue to spend on the race for Senate in Georgia despite the polls is Rick Jackson, the Republican gubernatorial nominee who appears to have closed his polling gap with Democratic nominee Keisha Lance Bottoms, The Sun’s Al Weaver reports. “They’re all tied together, and the turnout operations, for sure, are linked in many cases because governors a lot of times have really good ground games,” Senate Majority Leader John Thune told The Sun.

GOP Senate watchers consider wins by New Hampshire Gov. Kelly Ayotte and Texas Gov. Greg Abbott in their respective races as a key factor in winning the Senate races in those states. Both sitting Republican governors are up in public polls (Ayotte is way up). One place where the connection goes the other way: Michigan, where Republicans worry that a poor showing by the party’s gubernatorial nominee, Rep. John James, could be a drag on Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers.

More: Ken Paxton’s Ex-Wife Says She’s Voting for Ken Paxton — Without Mentioning Ken Paxton

FROM ST. MATTHEW’S CATHEDRAL 


A fire-engine red program with an image of John Carroll, the first Roman Catholic bishop in the United States, and clergy donning red vestments greeted worshipers at the 74th Red Mass yesterday — an annual service held ahead of the Supreme Court's term to “beseech the blessings of the Holy Spirit” onto those in the legal field.

Supreme Court Chief Justice John Roberts, Justices Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett and former Justice Anthony Kennedy sat in the front, with Vice President JD Vance, and second lady Usha Vance seated a few pews behind with their children in tow. “America the Beautiful” rang through the cathedral before the clergy processed out.

The now-blessed high court will hear oral arguments today in a case that could block one of the last remaining legal paths for holding fossil fuel companies responsible for damage from climate change, The Sun’s Mara Hoplamazian reports. The case, Suncor Energy v. Boulder County, will decide if federal law precludes lawsuits against companies in state courts for costs associated with climate disasters.

More: Alito Defends Justices Against a ‘Concerted Effort to Intimidate the Court’





NEW ON THE WASHINGTON SUN

Elections officials are still prepped for a bumpy ride, The Sun’s Adora Brown reports. Even after courts pushed back on Trump administration efforts to restrict mail-in voting, and top officials’ denials that there are plans to flood polling places with federal agents, Adora writes that blue state officials are still very wary. “In the event that something unusual or unexpected or alarming occurs, we have procedures in place to elevate that problem to our office,” Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows (D) told The Sun.

entries.title: Republicans Are Hoping Popular Governors Will Boost Their Senate Chances
entries.summary: “There’s always a connection,” Senate Majority Leader John Thune said of the impact of governor’s races on battleground Senate contests.
entries.content:
Senate Republicans are looking for some help come November in the form of key governor’s races that could make or break their hopes of retaining control of the upper chamber.

Even though most of the Senate contests are in friendly states to Republicans, the party’s incumbents and other candidates are swimming against the tide, with polls showing many of them trailing less than a month out.

Luckily for some of them, they could be buoyed by sitting governors who are also on the ballot and in pole position to nab another term.

“They’re all tied together, and the turnout operations, for sure, are linked in many cases because governors a lot of times have really good ground games,” said Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-South Dakota). “There’s always a connection.”

Atop that list are New Hampshire Gov. Kelly Ayotte and Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, who are considered key factors to potential Senate victories in the states.

Ayotte, a former Republican senator herself, is widely viewed as the preeminent reason that former Sen. John Sununu (R-New Hampshire) could score a return trip to Washington in his race against Rep. Chris Pappas (D-New Hampshire). A recent New York Times/Siena College poll recently showed her leading Democrat Cinde Warmington by 11 percentage points and topping 50 percent.

Pappas leads Sununu by 5percentage points in the same survey. Nevertheless, Republicans believe that the race represents one of their best opportunities to flip a seat, along with Michigan.

“Having a strong top of the ticket helps everybody on the ticket,” said Sen. Pete Ricketts (R-Nebraska), a former two-term governor. He also rattled off a state from his tenure as chairman of the Republican Governor’s Association: If a sitting governor won, the Senate candidate did also 75 percent of the time. “Correlation, not causation.”

Abbott, the longest-serving governor currently in office, has won all three of his contests by double digits, and has shown an ability to help out a down-ballot senator in a tough race. Abbott won his first reelection in 2018 by 13 percentage points — helping to drag Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) across the finish line against former Democratic Rep. Beto O’Rourke.

This year may be different. Abbott only holds a low-to-mid single digit lead over Democrat Gina Hinojosa. Even so, few Republicans believe he is in peril and argue that his ground operation and fundraising prowess will boost state Attorney General Ken Paxton in his senate bid. As of the end of June, Abbott had about $67 million in his cash on hand compared to only $3 million for Hinojosa.

“The governor’s race is critically important,” Cruz told The Washington Sun. “Greg Abbott’s going to be reelected. He’s done a terrific job as governor, and he’s raised a lot of money, which he’s going to deploy to turn voters out.”

“There’s no doubt Texas is competitive right now, and it is far too close for comfort,” he said, adding that he still believes Paxton will defeat Democrat James Talarico.

There are limits to Abbott’s reach. Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) noted that on the physical ballot itself, the Senate race will be leading the ticket, with the respective House and the governor races following in sequential order.

There are other states where a governor candidate is hanging tough, but may not be able to pull the Republican Senate candidate along enough.

In Georgia’s governor’s race, Republican Rick Jackson is suddenly running neck and neck with former Democratic Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms, having been buoyed by a significant financial advantage on the airways. However, Republican Rep. Mike Collins has struggled to make inroads against incumbent Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff.

In some states, neither candidate seems likely to help the other: Republican Ohio Sen. Jon Husted and Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy face similar polling deficits.

A series of gubernatorial races in the Midwest may do Republicans little favor — and in some cases, serious harm.

In Michigan, Democratic Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson holds a commanding advantage in the governor’s race against Republican Rep. John James, one that Republicans are worried could affect former Republican Rep. Mike Rogers in his bid to topple Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in the Senate race.

“That’s a big problem,” said one Republican operative who’s worked on Senate races, requesting anonymity to discuss races. “How much are we going to lose the governor’s race by? How’s that math going to work out?

One Republican operative argued that James, who has already dropped two statewide contests in recent years, could afford to lose the race by roughly 7 or 8 percentage points and leave Rogers with a shot.

“Anything more, and it becomes damn near impossible to close that gap,” a second Republican operative said on a condition of anonymity to frankly discuss the state of play.

In Iowa, Democrat Rob Sand is leading Republican Zach Lahn in the governor’s race. However, Senate candidate and incumbent Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson is considered to be in a stronger position than Rogers.

Hinson has shown signs of concern in recent weeks, including her call for President Donald Trump to end the war in Iran amid sky-high gas and diesel prices that have plagued the region.

Like Texas, Iowa lists Senate races at the top of the physical ballot. Republicans think Hinson could boost her fellow Republicans.

“Ashley is going to pull everybody up,” said Sen. Joni Ernst (R-Iowa), who Hinson and Democrat Josh Turek are seeking to replace. “I don’t know that the impact of the governor’s race will hurt Ashley at all.”
entries.author: Al Weaver

entries.title: Republicans in Safe Red States Are Breaking With Trump, Too
entries.summary: At least five GOP senators who are not on the ballot have criticized the president’s handling of the economy and policy priorities.
entries.content:
It’s not just vulnerable Republicans in swing districts distancing themselves from their party leader.

As President Donald Trump travels the country touting the “greatest” American economy in history, even senators in safe red states are beginning to push back on his rhetoric and policies.

“I'm not going to tell the voters, ‘Oh, it's President Biden's fault, and it's not that bad, you shouldn’t believe your checkbooks,’” Sen. John Kennedy, whose home state of Louisiana swung for Trump by 22 points in 2024, told reporters before the Senate recessed for the elections.

“I also tell them the truth: The main reason for the resurgence in inflation is the Iran war. I think they appreciate the truth, but they’re angry,” Kennedy told The Washington Sun later. His term is up in 2028.

Such rhetoric is a surprising twist. Candidates in tough races often break with unpopular presidents, as they are doing this year. Lawmakers who aren’t on the ballot or who occupy safe seats seldom do. But suddenly they are, as if their states might not be as sheltered from the political headwinds sweeping the nation as history suggests, or perhaps they see hints that the winds could keep blowing for the rest of Trump’s term and beyond.

Kennedy is just one example of out-of-cycle Republicans increasingly criticizing Trump as his approval rating continues to drop. At least four other non-threatened GOP senators have split with the president in recent weeks.

Take West Virginia Sen. Jim Justice, who echoed Kennedy’s concerns that voters are frustrated by the cost of living. He told The Washington Sun that “Republicans,” not just the president, have made missteps while speaking with Americans about the economy.

West Virginia favored Trump by over 40 points and Justice’s term is not up until 2031.

“The power bills are high, diesel fuel’s off the chart, gasoline's off the chart, groceries are up,” he said.

He added that Republicans need to do a better job of messaging on the war in Iran, in particular. If he were president, Justice said he would hold fireside chats to more candidly discuss the reasons behind, and the economic consequences of, the war.

“I would be saying to them: ‘Here was the strategy, here’s what we accomplished,’” Justice said. “We knew that there was a real chance that it would drive gasoline and diesel and fertilizer and all that kind of stuff. We knew that and everything, but we never really dreamed we'd be there this long.”

The economy and war aren’t the only issues on which Republicans have countered the president. Senate Majority Leader John Thune began last week criticizing a slate of Trump campaign ads that seem to have been financed with taxpayer money.

“It’s a great message. I like the message. It shouldn’t have been paid for by taxpayer dollars,” Thune said.

Fellow South Dakota Sen. Mike Rounds also denounced the administration’s political advertisements, in addition to the clawback of nearly $1 billion in funding approved by Congress, as well as Trump’s executive action to temporarily expand the import of foreign beef.

When asked by The Sun what spurred his various recent breaks with the president, who won South Dakota by nearly 30 points in 2024, Rounds threw his hands up and shrugged.

Rounds, who is up for reelection this year, pointed to Trump’s announcement on beef imports as a catalyst. Ranching and meatpacking are important industries in South Dakota

“He just recently announced it,” Rounds said. “That’s when we started discussing it. It’s based upon the actions where they were suggesting that they wanted to import beef at a time in which we should be making an American-first push.”

Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) has also been a loud critic of some of the president’s recent political moves, though Trump won Utah by nearly 22 points in 2024 and Curtis is not on the ballot until 2030.

Much like Rounds, Curtis decried Trump’s funding rescissions and taxpayer-funded advertisements. Most notably, he asked the Senate Judiciary Committee to investigate Donald Trump Jr. for taking money from a Russian oligarch to pay for some of his wedding festivities last month.

“Believe this, a Russian oligarch paid for a lavish wedding afterparty for Donald Trump Jr.,” Curtis said in a direct-to-camera social media video. “To me, it just stinks. It's corruption. I don’t like it.”

Curtis released another video Friday, saying Republicans have not done enough to tackle the cost of living. “We’ve not addressed what all of you care about so deeply, and that’s affordability,” Curtis said, recounting the price of gas across his state. “We just have not done a good job.”

Whether those Republicans are bracing for an even more hostile political environment coming their way is an open question, but several typically safe seats have recently become more competitive. Trump won Alaska by 13 points, Ohio by 11 and Texas by 14 in 2024, yet the Republican Party and its allies are spending heavily in those states this year.

That may have caught other politicians’ attention.

“The trend downwards is very clear," David Karol, a government professor at the University of Maryland, told The Sun. “It’s something that they know and that they’re aware of, and to the extent it makes Trump weaker, it makes people feel more free to separate themselves from some of his particularly unpopular decisions or actions.”

Trump himself seems concerned enough that he is planning rallies in solid-red states like Oklahoma and Alabama in the coming weeks. And some of the lawmakers who have distanced themselves from Trump, including Kennedy, have alluded to their own presidential ambitions.

Still, Sen. Thom Tillis (R-North Carolina), who has repeatedly clashed with the president throughout Trump’s second term and who is retiring this year, told The Sun that he wouldn’t consider these breaks to be a “sea change,” noting that most Senate Republicans have consistently voted alongside the president.

Tillis supports those Republicans separating themselves from Trump, though.

“It's people really expressing their differences, which I've encouraged,” Tillis said. “Because I actually believe that independence and having that image of independence going into this election is critically important to getting Republicans reelected. It’s a simple, practical matter.”

Karol chalked up the rise in part to timing. Trump had an outsized influence in this year’s primaries, successfully ousting Republican lawmakers who had broken with him in the past. Those contests are over, but 2028 still isn’t quite on the horizon yet, Karol said.

“Trump doesn't want criticism, but to criticize a policy position that is not something that is necessarily near and dear to his heart in a respectful way, I think it's survivable,” Karol said. “2028 is a long way off.”

entries.title: State Officials Are Trying to Get Ahead of Federal Agents at the Polls
entries.summary: The Trump administration has left open the door to sending federal agents to polling locations on Election Day.
entries.content:
Democratic state officials and organizations across the country are preparing for a scenario in which the Trump administration deploys federal agents to the polls in November.

The administration has said it has no plans to send federal agents to polling locations on Election Day. But President Donald Trump and some of his close advisers have left voting rights organizations and state officials uneasy after deflecting when asked about whether they will be deployed.

“The deployment of federal power against its opponents and organizations and the public is really top of mind right now,” said EJ Juárez, executive director of the State Innovation Exchange, a network of progressive state legislators across the country. “We have a set of people in power that are very much set on changing the rules of the game midway through.”

Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told lawmakers during a hearing in March that he would only send agents to the polls if there was a “specific threat,” but that he couldn’t “guarantee hypothetically what threat would be.” When asked Monday by Time magazine whether he would deploy federal agents, Trump said, “Haven't thought of it.” He also refused to rule out using the Insurrection Act to declare a state of emergency leading up to the election.

“In the event that something unusual or unexpected or alarming occurs, we have procedures in place to elevate that problem to our office,” Shenna Bellows, Maine’s Democratic secretary of state, told The Washington Sun. “In collaboration with the attorney general's office, we would be in court and getting orders from the court within hours, not days or months.”

Bellows’ office has been working with state and local officials nationwide through the Elections Infrastructure Information Sharing and Analysis Center, a component of the nonprofit Center for Internet Security. In February 2025, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency cut $10 million that Congress had appropriated to CIS, directly impacting the EI-ISAC's work.

EI-ISAC was created in 2018 after elections were classified by the Department of Homeland Security as critical infrastructure. Election officials typically use it on Election Day as a situation room to share threat information, including threats from foreign adversaries. The November midterms will be the first major election without the federal government’s financial support or participation in the situation room.

Attorneys generals are working with election officials to get ahead of any attempts by the administration to send federal agents to the polls. Several sources who spoke with The Sun emphasized that this scenario could be illegal because federal laws state voters cannot be intimidated at the polls and armed federal agents cannot be present there.

“We've been doing the tabletop exercises not just between our office and the Michigan secretary of state and the governor's office and Michigan State Police, but also with local communities,” Democratic Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel said at a press briefing in September. “Community after community after community, we are sitting down and we are planning so that we can be ready for any set of circumstances that arises.”

Organizations are preparing programs and response networks to reassure voters in response to Trump administration rhetoric that elections aren’t secure.

The White House directed The Sun to a February news conference with then-White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt, who said she couldn’t guarantee that an ICE agent wouldn’t be around a polling location, but that the president had no formal plans to deploy them.

The Department of Defense responded to a letter from Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Michigan) asking whether federal agents would be deployed to the polls.

“The Department has no plan to deploy active-duty troops or Federalized National Guard to polling sites, nor does it have any plan to interfere with ballots, voting machines, or other election-related materials,” Assistant Secretary of Defense Mark Ditlevson wrote in his response.

In Tennessee, the city of Memphis has had a steady presence of federal police, immigrant enforcement agents and the National Guard as a part of an anti-crime task force the president launched last fall.

Ian Randolph, director of the Shelby County Voter Alliance, a coalition of non-partisan voting rights groups that works to turn out the vote, told The Sun that the tast force “had a deleterious effect” on turnout for primary voting and related events.

“It is not beyond us thinking that ICE or the federal police or the National Guard won't show up at some of our polls here in Memphis, even if it's just to sit out there,” Randolph said.

In some key areas, such a dampening effect on voter turnout could have serious implications for the most competitive races this midterm season.

The Save America Movement, a political organization based in Washington, D.C., that opposes the Trump administration, is planning to send a coalition of community members — including figures like clergy, nurses, teachers and veterans — to Mecklenburg County in North Carolina, Wayne County in Michigan, DeKalb County in Georgia and Cuyahoga County in Ohio. Community members trained in “de-escalation, deterrence and documentation” will be present at those polling locations.

Co-founder Mary Corcoran said the organization chose the counties based on the high-profile races there. She said she also asked herself, “What would Stephen Miller do?”

“These counties have robust immigrant populations. Black, Latino and Asian populations,” Corcoran told The Sun. “Even if a small percentage of those voters that turned out in the last midterm election were intimidated into not showing up this year, it could have an impact on the outcome of the statewide races in those states.”

entries.title: Ken Paxton Blames D.C. for His Campaign Messaging in a Leaked Recording
entries.summary: “I’ve never been in a race where I felt less control over the campaign,” he said, according to audio obtained by Politico.
entries.content:
Texas Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton privately complained last month that Washington is driving the messaging around his campaign, saying he has little control over his own race.

“I’ve never been in a race where I felt less control over the campaign and, like, what issues are going to matter because it’s all coming — you know — from D.C.,” Paxton said at a private fundraiser on Sept. 24, according to audio obtained by Politico.

“I don’t control message or what we’re doing.”

The comments are the second set to emerge from the fundraiser in Washington. Audio released last week captured Paxton blaming President Donald Trump’s midterm convention in Dallas for a decline in his poll numbers.

In the new recording, Paxton said Texas’ size makes it difficult to reach voters himself, leaving much of the campaign messaging to others.

“But then it comes down to your messaging,” Paxton said, “which in a federal race comes from other people a lot of times, which you don’t control.”

Paxton campaign adviser Nick Maddux told Politico that Paxton was referring to independent groups supporting his campaign.

“Campaigns don’t coordinate with super PACS and that’s obviously what AG Paxton was referring to,” Maddux said.

Those groups are playing an outsized role in Paxton’s race against the Democratic nominee, state Rep. James Talarico. Republicans spent $122 million supporting Paxton in September and had another $66 million in airtime reserved through Election Day as of last week, according to AdImpact data reported by The Texas Tribune. Paxton’s campaign accounted for just $1.2 million of the Republican spending in September.

Texas PAC, a group connected to Senate Majority Leader John Thune, had spent $131 million on the race as of last week, while Trump’s super PAC had spent nearly $24 million, according to the Tribune. Paxton has since launched his own $20 million advertising campaign.

Paxton’s private assessment of the race has repeatedly clashed with the confidence Trump has projected publicly.

Paxton also spent much of the Republican primary against Sen. John Cornyn attacking Washington’s influence and the outside money backing his opponent. Trump endorsed Paxton over Cornyn a week before the May runoff, which Paxton went on to win.

Paxton now faces Talarico with less than a month until Election Day. A New York Times/Siena poll conducted Sept. 21 through Sept. 30 found Talarico leading Paxton 51% to 45% among 615 likely voters, with a margin of error of 4.5 percentage points. Other recent public polls have also shown a close race.

entries.title: Karoline Leavitt Has a New Job at Fox News
entries.summary: She’s taking the new gig just two months after leaving the Trump administration.
entries.content:
Former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt is taking a new job at Fox News just two months after leaving the Trump administration.

Leavitt, 29, will start Nov. 1 as an on-air contributor and appear across the network’s news and opinion programming, the network announced Monday morning.

Leavitt left the White House at the end of August, saying she wanted to spend more time with her family after giving birth to her second child in May. At the time, Trump said she would remain an outside adviser and a key voice in Republican politics.

Her hiring puts another former Trump press secretary at Fox. Kayleigh McEnany joined the network after serving in the same job during Trump’s first term.

“Karoline’s firsthand experience in the White House and on the presidential campaign trail gives her a distinct understanding of today’s political landscape,” Fox News Media CEO Suzanne Scott said in a statement.

The announcement also comes as President Donald Trump continues to attack Fox over coverage he dislikes. Last week, Trump accused the network of repeating “a completely negative narrative” and said “MAGA, and REAL Patriots, will never like Fox!”

Leavitt was the youngest person to serve as White House press secretary. She became one of Trump’s most visible defenders, frequently sparring with reporters during White House briefings.

Leavitt has since moved with her family to New Hampshire, where she grew up. She said she plans to bring Fox viewers “the unique perspective and candor that defined my tenure with the Trump administration.”

entries.title: Soldiers Wounded in Iranian Drone Strike Say They Aren't Getting Proper Care
entries.summary: After years of U.S. drawdown in the Middle East, the region does not have any major American-run medical facilities.
entries.content:
The shrapnel hit Army Lt. Col. Arturo Lincón's body like shattered glass.

One chunk of metal lodged into the left side of his jaw. Another piece sliced through his salivary gland before bouncing off his jaw and piercing the back of his neck, severing an artery and embedding in a vertebra.

Lincón was among dozens of U.S. soldiers injured in an Iranian drone strike on March 1. The attack on the second day of the U.S. war with Iran killed six troops who were providing logistical support of critical supplies at Port Shuaiba in Kuwait.

Whether the military was properly prepared for treating its wounded has become a sharp point of contention. Soldiers and family members have told The Associated Press of a failure to recognize the seriousness of injuries, a poor plan to get the wounded to hospitals and red tape that has hindered follow-up care. The Pentagon has said that the medical care was appropriate.

Nine U.S. service members who were wounded spoke to the AP on the record — rare for troops still in the Army — about what they describe as a medical system that left them in many ways fighting to get treatment on their own.

The medical care was just one of the military’s failures stemming from the Port Shuaiba attack that soldiers described to the AP. The Army declined to comment on the AP's reporting, saying it had not yet briefed the families of those killed on the outcome of its investigation into the attack. The Pentagon also declined to comment.

The soldiers’ criticism comes against the backdrop of years of disinvestment and drawdowns in the Middle East by multiple administrations and political leaders who sought to end U.S. involvement in the region. Those choices left the region without any major U.S.-run medical facilities.
Iran US Port Shuaiba Attack (1719x1146, AR: 1.50)Lincón's wounds included a damaged left vertebral artery, which supplies blood to the brain, and put him at risk for a stroke. That was not considered by the Army to be serious enough to be admitted to Landstuhl Regional Medical Center in Germany, a major U.S. military facility, even though Lincón said a nurse there marveled that he was alive.

Instead he was sent to the nearby Army barracks and told to schedule outpatient appointments.

“I was just kind of on my own, at least it felt like that,” said Lincón, a veteran of wars in Iraq and Afghanistan.

Lincón's was not an isolated case.

Another soldier who had shrapnel removed from his head, Maj. Stephen Ramsbottom, said he waited over four months to receive his MRI results.

“I’ve had to build my own case for everything,” Ramsbottom told the AP. “It’s very frustrating.”

Soldiers helped save each other after Iranian attack

After the deadly drone strike, soldiers, who are equipped with tourniquets and trained in first aid, tended to each other and then searched on Google to race the wounded to the nearest hospital in Kuwait City about 20 minutes away.

Some of the most seriously wounded soldiers were medically evacuated from Kuwait within two days. Lincón, who was only about 7 feet (2.1 meters) from the blast, spent a week hospitalized there where he had surgery to remove shrapnel from his jaw. He said medical staff told him he had a traumatic brain injury from the force of the blast that ruptured his eardrum and left him briefly blinded.

Chief Warrant Officer 4 Rodney Bearman, who had shrapnel embedded from his face to his legs, and some of the other soldiers who were briefly seen at Kuwaiti medical facilities were sent to the homes of U.S. government employees. Iran had unleashed missiles and drones that made it risky for evacuation flights.

Some 10 days after the attack, the soldiers were loaded onto a cargo plane. They sat on the floor with straps, including Bearman, who could barely eat or lie down.
Iran US Port Shuaiba Attack Wounded (1600x1200, AR: 1.33)When they arrived in Germany, Bearman said they learned they were not documented as wounded in combat and would not be hospitalized at Landstuhl. Instead, they were sent to the barracks, as Lincón had been, and told to get outpatient care. Bearman said they were documented that way due to a coding error.

“Never did I think that if I was wounded that these things would happen,” said Bearman, who has served for over three decades, including in Afghanistan. “Some sacred trust that I thought would never be broken was broken.”

Lincón says he went days without pain medication. He carried a CD with a copy of medical records from Kuwait that he showed the ER doctor at Landstuhl who expressed concern that he had not been evaluated yet by a trauma team.

Pentagon says all wounded troops are evaluated

Soldiers may not be aware of initial evaluations, like the Army’s battlefield concussion evaluation, that focus on identifying symptoms such as double vision or repeated vomiting and other observations. Troops with mild TBIs and hit by shrapnel often returned to duty quickly in Iraq and Afghanistan. Many soldiers who spoke to the AP did not know the severity of their TBIs.

A Pentagon official told the AP that Landstuhl’s mission, especially in battlefield casualty situations, is focused on stabilizing patients to transfer them for more specialized care at a military hospital in the U.S. rather than admitting them.

Meanwhile, large hospitals closer to Kuwait have been shuttered. For example, Air Force Theater Hospital at Joint Base Balad in Iraq was handed over to the Iraqi government in 2011 as part of drawdown efforts.

In a statement, the Pentagon said that all wounded troops who arrive at its medical facilities are evaluated and may be admitted based on the severity of the injury according to physicians who follow "healthcare-industry practices.”

After about a week in Germany, many of the injured soldiers were sent to Fort Hood in Texas, where they underwent the Army's demobilization process to return deployed troops home.

Medical records shared with the AP by Ramsbottom and another officer show they were not diagnosed with TBIs until Fort Hood. The officer, who was blown off his chair, said he did not get care for weeks after that diagnosis and had to identify the specialists he needed, like a neuro-ophthalmologist to diagnose the blurred vision from his TBI rather than counting on the military’s medical system.

Maj. Billy Key says he did not get specialized care until mid-April when he was sent to a U.S. soldier recovery unit to be treated for his head injury, hearing loss and the smoke inhalation that damaged his lungs.

“It took too long,” he said.

Dr. James Kelly, chief medical scientist at the Invisible Wounds Foundation, which is focused on military brain injuries, said it’s still not uncommon for a TBI diagnosis to take longer than it should, which could impact a soldier getting treatment as early as possible for the best outcome.

“It’s disappointing but not surprising,” said Kelly, an emeritus professor of neurology at the University of Colorado School of Medicine. “In a war scenario, it goes on a fair bit.”

An initial thorough check should be done by a medically trained person, not simply another soldier, he said. Kelly said that too often medical records note only a concussion, which is in fact a mild TBI, but can be overlooked.

Many soldiers are struggling months after the attack

Lincón spent seven weeks getting specialized outpatient care at Walter Reed National Military Medical Center in Maryland, before being sent home to Kansas. Shrapnel is still in his back because it was too close to his spinal cord to remove without risking being left paralyzed. He struggles with dizziness that disrupts his life, he said.

He was awarded the Purple Heart and is back on active duty as an instructor at Fort Leavenworth. But his troubles continued beyond medical care.

Lincón, who was born in Texas to Mexican parents, was issued only a temporary one-year passport after his passport was blown up in the attack and he was asked for additional documentation to prove his U.S. citizenship. After the AP reached out to the State Department to inquire about his case, the 1995 West Point graduate said he received a call saying the request for more information was a mistake and he would be receiving a passport that would be good for 10 years.

“I’m American enough to have fought in three different wars," Lincón said.

He’s also concerned his medical records are incomplete. His claim for Traumatic Injury benefits under the Servicemembers' Group Life Insurance was denied due to not meeting the threshold for hearing loss, though it never addressed his other issues, he said. The program gives cash to service members who suffer severe injuries.

The Army's Human Resources Command did not immediately respond to an email from the AP asking for an explanation.

“I’m fortunate to survive and that’s how I look at it,” Lincón said. “That’s the only way to look at it at this point.”

Watson reported from San Diego, Brook from New Orleans and Toropin from Washington. Associated Press journalist Nicholas Ingram in Ankeny, Iowa, contributed to this report.

entries.title: D.C. Plans to Spend $72,000 on Historic Preservation of Black Neighborhoods
entries.summary: The D.C. Office of Planning can spend the grant on a new nomination to the National Register of Historic Places.
entries.content:
The National Park Service has awarded the D.C. government funding for the historic preservation of Black neighborhoods.

The Park Service announced the $72,000 underrepresented communities grant to the D.C. Office of Planning in a news release late last week. The grant will fund historic surveying, multiple property documentation, and “National Register Nominations for Historically Black Neighborhoods in Washington, D.C.”

The D.C. Office of Planning did not respond to a request for comment.

The award is among 16 other projects across 15 states, totaling nearly $1.18 million. The grants are issued through the Historic Preservation Fund to help states, tribes, local governments and nonprofits expand listings in the National Register of Historic Places.

To qualify for the grant, the project must result in a new nomination to the national historic place registry or amend an existing registered historic place nomination to include underrepresented communities.

Other projects included $100,000 sent to the state of Maryland to nominate and survey Black churches and cemeteries in Baltimore for historic place listings.

Last year, the D.C. Preservation League earned a $75,000 underappreciated community grant for multiple property documentation and “National Register Nominations of Washington, D.C. LGBTQ+ Resources,” but the Trump administration stripped that funding after reallocating historic preservation funds away from LGBTQ projects, the Washington Blade reported.

entries.title: Disgraced Former House Speaker Dennis Hastert Dies at 84
entries.summary: The Illinois congressman, who was speaker from 1999 until 2007, died of natural causes at his home.
entries.content:
By Michael Tarm and Herbert G. McCann

CHICAGO (AP) — Dennis Hastert, the nation’s longest-serving Republican House speaker, who helped turn much of President George W. Bush’s agenda into law before his own political legacy was forever fouled by allegations that he molested high school athletes when he was a wrestling coach, died over the weekend, a coroner said Monday. He was 84.

Hastert, who was speaker from 1999 until 2007, died of natural causes at his home, according to Kendall County Coroner Jacquie Purcell.

When he was sentenced in 2016 to more than a year behind bars, the former history teacher became one of the highest-ranking American politicians ever ordered to prison.

In the late 1990s, Hastert was a little-known Illinois lawmaker with a reputation for congeniality that had helped him ascend the ranks of congressional leaders. When Newt Gingrich lost support because of ethics violations and the GOP’s poor showing in an election, Republicans elected Hastert to succeed him. In his first weeks on the job, he presided over the House while the Senate conducted Bill Clinton’s impeachment trial.

After the GOP reclaimed the White House, Hastert took much of what Bush proposed and steered it to passage, including massive tax cuts and a measure that amounted to a huge expansion of prescription drug benefits — the biggest change in Medicare in decades.

His legacy was suddenly thrown into doubt in 2015, when he was accused of evading banking regulations as part of a plan to pay hush money to conceal unspecified "prior misconduct." Nearly a year later, prosecutors filed papers that described what media reports had suggested for months: Hastert’s misconduct involved the sexual abuse of teenage boys on his wrestling team in the small town of Yorkville, west of Chicago.

During a 16-year coaching career, he led his team to a state championship and was named national coach of the year in 1976. But behind the accolades, prosecutors said, Hastert sexually abused at least four team members from 1965 to 1981.

The person Hastert was paying, identified in court papers only as Individual A, said the abuse occurred in a motel room when he was 14 on the way home from wrestling camp. Hastert allegedly touched other wrestlers in a locker room after saying he would give them massages. Two wrestlers said Hastert performed sex acts on them.

Prosecutors also described a recliner where Hastert often sat in the locker room with a direct view of the stalls where the boys showered.

Hastert agreed to plead guilty to evading banking laws. In all, he paid more than $1.7 million out of $3.5 million that he had promised to Individual A, sometimes in lump sums of $100,000 cash.

At the sentencing hearing where he received 15 months behind bars, the visibly angry judge called Hastert a “serial child molester.” A former wrestler struggled with his emotions as he told the court about his “dark secret” from adolescence.

In his own statement, Hastert said he was “deeply ashamed” and admitted that he "mistreated” some of his athletes. But he never referred directly to sexual abuse.

The public knew nothing about Hastert’s past when Republicans lost seats in the 1998 midterm elections. Hastert confronted Gingrich about dissatisfaction in the GOP ranks, saying it was unlikely Gingrich could hold his post, Hastert wrote in "Speaker: Lessons from 40 Years in Coaching and Politics."

"Well, I'll make them support me," he quoted Gingrich saying of the GOP rebels. Told that was unlikely, Gingrich asked Hastert what to do.

"Do what you have to do," he replied. The next day, Gingrich stepped down as speaker and left the House.

Hastert’s path to the speaker’s office was cleared when Louisiana Rep. Bob Livingston, who was considered a lock to replace Gingrich as speaker, resigned after acknowledging several extramarital affairs.

In January 1999, Hastert broke with tradition by delivering his acceptance speech from the House floor and by allowing Minority Leader Dick Gephardt, a Missouri Democrat, to briefly preside over the day's proceedings.

"Solutions to problems cannot be found in a pool of bitterness," Hastert said in his speech. "They can be found in an environment in which we trust one another's word, where we generate heat and passion, but where we recognize that each member is equally important to our overall mission of improving the life of the American people."

Hastert was aware of the personal pitfalls of holding the powerful position.

"You know, in this business, especially in a job like this, you can get your head someplace where it shouldn't be," Hastert said in a 1999 interview with The Associated Press. "But you come back home, and you're home. You're back where you've always been, and your feet are back on the ground."

He was generally viewed as a friendly, even-tempered lawmaker. His wrestling experience followed him to Washington, with GOP colleagues often calling him "coach.”

Hastert said he lacked the appetite for higher office.

As the recount of the 2000 presidential election dragged on, Hastert’s aides briefed him on the possibility that he might become acting president in the event of an Electoral College deadlock.

"I really didn't want to be president, temporary or otherwise," he wrote in his book. But he decided that he would not pass the office to the constitutional officer next in line if an Electoral College deadlock extended beyond Inauguration Day. In the end, the Supreme Court's 5-4 ruling ended the recount, and Bush moved into the White House.

Hastert’s journey to Congress from his boyhood farm appeared to be the result of fate and luck.

In 1980, he finished third in an Illinois House primary. But the incumbent became fatally ill, and GOP leaders chose Hastert to take his place on the November ballot, where he won in a traditional GOP stronghold.

Hastert became a congressional candidate in 1986, when local Republican leaders put him on the primary ballot, replacing freshman Rep. John Grotberg, who was battling cancer. Hastert went on to beat the Democrat with 52 percent of the vote, his smallest margin of victory in a congressional race.

In Washington, Hastert served quietly in House leadership, working closely with Gingrich and then-House Majority Whip Tom DeLay after Republicans took control in 1995. Several years later, DeLay was the force driving Clinton’s impeachment and was simply too toxic to seek the speaker’s chair.

Hastert’s tenure was marked by a shift of power from committee chairmen to GOP leaders, fealty to the Bush administration and an explosion of congressional pet projects known as earmarks. Democrats fumed that he weakened the ethics process that ensnared DeLay, who left Congress under a cloud of criminal charges in 2006.

Hastert became wealthy largely through a complex web of transactions that coincided with one of his own highway earmarks increasing the value of land he had purchased in his district.

He was forced to step down as speaker in 2007, when Democrats gained control of the House, and he resigned his seat later that year. In 2008, he joined the Washington lobbying firm of Dickstein Shapiro as a senior adviser, specializing in government law and strategy.

Born in Aurora, Illinois, Hastert earned a bachelor's degree in economics from Wheaton College in 1964 and a master’s in education from Northern Illinois University in 1967.

In 2007, Wheaton named its newly created public policy center the J. Dennis Hastert Center for Economics, Government and Public Policy. After Hastert’s indictment, the school removed his name in 2015. Other organizations abandoned associations with Hastert, and his portrait was removed from a hallway outside the House chamber.

Hastert lived his entire life in Chicago's suburbs, primarily in the Yorkville area. While growing up, he helped his father with the family feed business.

Survivors include his wife, Jean, and two adult sons.

entries.title: Kash Patel Gets Engaged to Country Singer Alexis Wilkins
entries.summary: The pair have been dating since before Patel took over as head of the FBI in 2025.
entries.content:
FBI Director Kash Patel is engaged to his country singer girlfriend, Alexis Wilkins, the pair announced in a post to X on Sunday evening.

Wilkins, 27, posted a black-and-white photo of herself standing with Patel, 46, flashing her hand in front of them to show off her ring with the caption, “Went and got the law involved.” The two have been dating since before Patel took over as head of the FBI in 2025, when she attended his swearing in.

The country singer and political commentator released her debut album in 2023. Wilkins has been affiliated with conservative groups and writes on her website that she “honors country tradition while adding relevance and current commentary.”

Patel, who reposted Wilkin's photo, has faced criticism for traveling on government aircraft on trips that have no known or apparent law enforcement purpose, including using an FBI jet to fly to State College, Pennsylvania, for a pro wrestling event where Wilkins performed the national anthem. Photos posted to social media by Wilkins afterward showed the couple smiling while she held an oversized golden championship belt.

Wilkins also made headlines as a performer at President Donald Trump's Great American State Fair on the National Mall as part of America 250, as other artists pulled out of the event after finding out it was not a non-partisan celebration.

entries.title: Spirit’s Win in Houston Has the Team on the Brink of a Third Straight Postseason
entries.summary: The Spirit have a chance to win the NWSL Shield, but need losses from the top two teams.
entries.content:
The Spirit are on the brink of clinching their third consecutive playoff appearance.

Washington defeated Houston 3–2 on Sunday to put them nine points above the playoff line with just three matches left. The Spirit currently sit in third place in the NWSL standings, trailing league-leader Gotham FC by six points and second-place San Diego Wave FC by two.

The Spirit’s next match is against Gotham on Oct. 17, which will have major playoff implications. A win or tie should secure a postseason berth for the team. Gotham FC tied Angel City 1–1 Sunday after surrendering an equalizer in stoppage time.

On Sunday, the Spirit dashed Houston’s playoff hopes, losing a one-goal lead twice before Clara Luvanga scored the game winner in the 84th minute. The loss eliminated the Dash from playoff contention.

The Spirit have four wins in their last six matches and play the fifth-place Kansas City Current on Oct. 25 before concluding the regular season against the Chicago Stars, who are last in the league, on Nov. 1.

For the Spirit to clinch the league's top record, they would need to win their remaining games, and Gotham and San Diego would both need to lose multiple matches. Both Washington and Gotham have similar schedules left, with one match against a team in playoff contention and one that isn’t, aside from the match against each other.

San Diego Wave FC has three remaining matches against the North Carolina Courage, Boston Legacy FC and Bay FC, all of which are eighth or lower in the league standings. It has possibly the easiest path to the NWSL Shield, which is awarded annually to the league’s top regular season team.

Perhaps a more realistic goal for the Spirit is clinching a home quarterfinal matchup, which is awarded to the teams that finish in the top four of the standings. The team has a five-point lead over Kansas City and is three points above fourth-place Utah, to clinch a home match in the postseason.

entries.title: WMATA Proposes Inflation-Based Metro Fare Increase
entries.summary: Officials project the fare increase would bring in an extra $40-45 million in revenue, while causing 8 million fewer trips.
entries.content:
Metro riders may have to pay higher fares in the coming years as the Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Authority wants to raise prices to keep up with inflation.

In a meeting Thursday, the WMATA Finance and Capital Committee will review a possible 11.1% inflation-based fare increase for Metrobus and Metrorail starting in fiscal 2028, according to board documents. The move, proposed by WMATA officials, would raise the cost of riding the Metro to between $2.50 and $7.50, up from the current $2.25 to $6.75 price range.

The fare hike would bring in an expected $40 million to $45 million more in revenue, while causing riders to take 8 million fewer trips, according to board documents. The proposal also outlines a framework to eliminate cash payments for bus travel in an effort to modernize the payment system.

“Collectively, both the proposed fare strategy and potential FY2028 fare changes are intended to improve customer convenience, support long-term revenue sustainability, enhance operational flexibility and position Metro for continued regional leadership in transit fare innovation,” WMATA’s proposal said.

The last time WMATA raised the fare was in 2024, increasing the price by 12.5%.

WMATA will also ask the committee to review a universal youth fare program that would offer all children ages 5 to 18 who live in the District, Maryland or Virginia free rides on the Metrobus and Metrorail. The proposal said that it would cost $7 million and add 900,000 trips.

The committee will not take any action on the proposal on Thursday. WMATA officials recommend the Metro Board of Directors schedule a public hearing to collect feedback before implementing the changes.

entries.title: Alex Ovechkin Says the 2026-27 NHL Season Will Be His Last
entries.summary: Ovechkin has spent his entire 22-year career with the Capitals.
entries.content:
This season will officially be Alex Ovechkin’s last.

On Monday, the Capitals’ captain said that he will retire at the end of the current NHL season, his 22nd with the organization. The announcement came on the 21-year anniversary of his NHL debut.

Ovechkin addressed his teammates in the locker room before the Capitals went public with the announcement, saying he and his family made the decision over the summer. The organization plans to honor Ovechkin on the eighth of each month this season. The left winger has worn the No. 8 his entire career.

“I love this game so much, but I know in my heart it’s the right decision,” Ovechkin said in a statement. “I am excited about this season with my teammates, and we will do everything we can to make this year special.”

The Capitals opened the season on Friday with a 5–2 win over the Hurricanes and lost on Saturday to the Lightning 3–1. The team’s home-opener on Wednesday is against the Penguins, who feature 39-year-old Sidney Crosby. Ovechkin and Crosby have widely been considered two of the greatest players of their generation.

Ovechkin is on the short list of greatest athletes in the history of D.C. He led the Capitals to the 2018 Stanley Cup title and broke numerous franchise and league records along the way, including Wayne Gretzky’s record for goals.

“For more than two decades, Alex has given our fans everything they could ask for: the goals, the records, the physicality, the passion, and an unmatched desire to win,” Capitals owner Ted Leonsis posted on X after the announcement.

The 41-year-old was selected No. 1 overall by the Capitals in the 2004 NHL draft and has a chance to add more milestones before he retires, including topping Gretzky’s record for combined goals (regular season and playoffs) and most assists in franchise history, among others.

A native of Russia, Ovechkin has also won three gold medals in the world championships and played in three Olympics while representing his country. Ovechkin drew criticism in September for appearing in a United Russia video advertisement supporting President Vladimir Putin.

He re-signed with the Capitals this summer on a one-year deal worth $4.25 million. He’s made nearly $175 million in career earnings, according to Spotrac.

The Capitals have a chance to send Ovechkin out as a winner. After missing the playoffs last season, the team had a strong offseason, adding forwards Alex Tuch and Jordan Kyrou, and center Boone Jenner to completely revamp the team’s offense around its aging star.

“We have a fucking unbelievable team this year,” Ovechkin told his teammates in his locker room announcement. “And have 82 games left. Let’s make the playoffs. Let’s have fun.”
