entries.title: Senator’s ‘Zombie' Campaign Committee Shuts Down 13 Years After His Death
entries.summary: Sen. Frank Lautenberg died in 2013, but his campaign apparatus lived on.
entries.content:
More than 13 years after Sen. Frank Lautenberg died, his Senate campaign committee has officially departed as well.

Lautenberg for Senate filed termination paperwork with the Federal Election Commission on Sunday, indicating it distributed about $87,000 in cash that had lingered in its account.

Most of that money — about $58,000 — went to the Lautenberg Foundation, a private, tax-exempt nonprofit that primarily makes modest grants to other nonprofits. Among them of late: the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, Planned Parenthood, George Washington University, Colgate University, Anti-Defamation League, Friends of the Israel Defense Forces, and the Conference of Presidents of Major American Jewish Organizations, according to IRS records.

“This foundation qualifies as a charitable organization … and no family members receive compensation from the foundation,” Lautenberg for Senate wrote in a memo to the FEC. A campaign representative couldn’t immediately be reached for comment.

The rest of Lautenberg for Senate’s residual funds went toward legal and consulting fees, records show.

The Washington Sun reported in April that Lautenberg for Senate began taking steps to unravel itself after more than a dozen years existing as a so-called “zombie campaign.”

That included forgiving a $1.09 million loan Lautenberg personally made to his old campaign committee — one that the committee never paid back and continued to carry on its books for years after the New Jersey Democrat had died in office in 2013 at age 89 while serving his fifth Senate term.

Defunct federal political campaigns with leftover cash have several options for their money, including donating it to charity, paying off “wind-down” expenses and disgorging it to the U.S. Treasury’s general fund.

But a few committees — including those led by dead politicians — have either sat on the cash for months or even years, or used the money for purposes that government watchdogs say violate the spirit, and potentially the letter, of laws prohibiting the personal use of campaign funds.

entries.title: MAHA Activists Feel Betrayed by the Farm Bill — And Their GOP Allies
entries.summary: The latest version of the farm bill pumps the brakes on some pesticide safety reviews and regenerative farming funding.
entries.content:
Leaders of the Make America Healthy Again movement aren’t happy with parts of this year’s version of the farm bill — or the lawmakers who had vowed to hear their concerns.

The latest version of the agriculture policy bill — supported by Republicans purporting to be MAHA sympathizers — falls short of the movement’s demands. Much of the focus is on pesticide safety reviews and potentially risks funding for a pilot program to back farming practices to improve soil health and limit pesticide use.

“That’s absolutely unethical and insane,” Zen Honeycutt, founder of Moms Across America, told The Washington Sun.

Honeycutt said she and her group have visited legislators in D.C. nearly every month for more than a year, advocating for restrictions on glyphosate, the most common pesticide used by farmers.

Kelly Ryerson, a MAHA activist who goes by the moniker “glyphosate girl,” hopes that if the Senate passes its version, lawmakers will hash out its differences with the House bill in a conference and scrap the pesticide measures.

Ryerson said she has been deeply disappointed by Republicans who had earlier appeared to sympathize with MAHA priorities, including those who formed MAHA caucuses in the House and the Senate at the outset of this Congress.

That includes Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kansas), chair of the Senate MAHA Caucus, who voted for the Senate bill in the Agriculture Committee, as did another caucus member, Tommy Tuberville (R-Alabama).

All the committee’s Republicans voted to block an amendment from Sen. Cory Booker (D-New Jersey) that would clarify that individuals can sue pesticide companies over health impacts, fueling fears among leading MAHA activists that their allies had been captured by big agricultural interests.

“Senator Marshall was supposed to be that person” to advocate for us, Ryerson said. “He is not.”

Marshall finds himself in a surprisingly competitive reelection race this year, when enthusiasm among rural voters for Republicans has dulled amid high input costs from the war in Iran and escalating trade wars with some of the country’s biggest buyers of American agriculture.

The MAHA movement, closely associated with Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., advocates for a range of issues, including cleaning up food and air and addressing the root causes of chronic health conditions. Stronger regulations on the pesticides farmers use on their crops is one of its most unifying issues, and it enjoys broad support from a majority of Americans.

Members of the MAHA caucuses have all voted for versions of the farm bill when given the opportunity, and some have voted specifically to protect pesticide makers from health-related lawsuits.

In April, pressure from MAHA activists successfully prompted the House to scrap from that chamber’s version of the farm bill a provision that would have added liability protections for pesticide manufacturers. Seven Republicans on the 14-member House MAHA Caucus voted against that amendment. The Senate version left out that provision.

Rep. Chellie Pingree (D-Maine) believes her colleagues in the House experienced the MAHA movement's power firsthand during that April vote, and it should not be underestimated. She said she believes Democrats didn't expect 73 Republicans to vote for the amendment.

“They seem to be a little slower to catch on in the Senate, but they haven’t had that same kind of amendment vote or experience we have,” Pingree said. But I think it’s a very durable issue, and we’re going to continue to see pressure on it.”

Alexandra Muñoz, an independent toxicologist who shares MAHA concerns about pesticides, said the bills still have “a lot of concerning provisions.” The measures would extend the deadline for a safety review of certain chemicals from 2026 to 2031. Other provisions would exclude certain chemicals from health and safety reviews altogether.

“Delaying or sidestepping these reviews will benefit the pesticide industry,” said Muñoz, who has testified against state laws protecting pesticide makers from lawsuits.

The Environmental Protection Agency is under an immense backlog of unfinished, legally mandated reviews for hundreds of older pesticides. Public health and environmental groups note that the agency has failed to finalize reviews for many widely used, high-volume conventional chemicals due to complex assessments involving endangered species and potential endocrine disruption.

The EPA is mandated to review pesticides every 15 years, with this current review cycle beginning in 2007. The agency already received a four-year extension in 2022.

Glyphosate is also at the center of the MAHA’s frustration with the EPA. The EPA says the chemical has low toxicity levels when used correctly, but studies on its long-term health impacts are mixed. Farmers have voiced concerns about their need for glyphosate, and a proposed ban in Illinois is expected to cost farmers around half a billion dollars in additional spending.

The Senate bill also shifts conservation funding to various programs prioritized by both sides of the Agriculture Committee, potentially moving funding away from a regenerative farming pilot program at the USDA that was expanded by an executive order President Donald Trump signed in June.

The USDA announced on Tuesday it would increase funding for this program from $700 million to $1 billion in 2027, saying it would advance the MAHA movement “by building a healthier, more resilient food system.”

Democrats are pushing to maintain current funding levels for all existing conservation programs, including the Environmental Quality Incentives Program and the Conservation Stewardship Program, as well as increased funding for programs set to receive a decrease in the farm bill.

“We’re seeing support from a broad coalition of farmers and consumers for these popular, voluntary conservation programs,” Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minnesota), ranking member of the Senate Agriculture Committee, said in a statement.

Tuberville told The Sun he had not heard any concerns from MAHA groups, and that he believed the farm bill was “all set.” Marshall did not respond to questions from The Sun.

Some agriculture-focused Republicans are more outwardly skeptical of MAHA’s intentions, with some arguing MAHA groups and influencers don’t understand the needs of farmers and want to slow the farm bill from passing.

“They don’t even know what a pesticide is,” said Sen. Jim Justice of West Virginia. “All they're doing is trying to throw a crescent wrench in the middle of the engine while the engine's running.”

Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa), a farmer and longtime outspoken voice on agriculture issues, said he has not heard of desired changes from the MAHA groups.

The Senate has given no indication of when it might take up on the floor what would be the first full five-year farm bill since 2018. Farmers who have faced inflation over the past six years are desperate for updated commodity prices. The Senate Agriculture Committee passed the bill on a party-line vote, but it needs 60 votes to pass out of the Senate floor.

entries.title: Supreme Court Wrestles With Future of Climate Change Cases
entries.summary: The justices asked questions about whether local governments can hold fossil fuel companies responsible for climate disasters.
entries.content:
The Supreme Court grappled Monday over the future of state lawsuits seeking to hold fossil fuel companies accountable for the costs of climate change.

In nearly two hours of oral arguments in the case, Suncor vs. Boulder, the justices focused on a procedural question over whether fossil fuel companies must face lawsuits over climate damages in state court, or if federal law precludes them.

Climate change itself was not front and center, but the case could be one of the biggest of the new term.

The city and county of Boulder filed a state lawsuit in 2018, aiming to hold Suncor Energy and Exxon Mobil responsible for costs associated with climate disasters, such as fires and floods, arguing that those companies deceived the public about the dangers of their products.

The state lawsuits are one of the few ways forward for states and local governments seeking to address global warming and its effects, but an attorney for the fossil fuel companies told the justices that billions of dollars are at stake in similar lawsuits whose futures could be determined by the court’s ruling.

The justices did little to clarify Monday if they would allow the claim to move forward. The justices across the bench agreed the case was “complicated.”

Justice Brett Kavanaugh indicated his concern about the potential economic fallout of state climate lawsuits, saying a lawyer representing the city and county of Boulder was being cavalier about the issues that could arise.

“It’s going to bankrupt, you know, if there are enough of these, bankrupt these various defendants and certainly other defendants out there,” he said.

But other Republican-appointed justices seemed more ambiguous in their thinking on the case.

Chief Justice John Roberts noted that there are situations where issues that happen outside of a particular state are allowed to be litigated in that state, comparing it to litigation over the internet.

“I guess I’m not quite sure what makes this situation different from all those other ones where we’ve allowed them to proceed in state court,” Roberts said.

At the same time, Roberts characterized Boulder’s lawsuit as an “effort to reduce emissions,” a point lawyers for the fossil fuel companies have argued.

Justice Samuel Alito, who owns stock in fossil fuel companies that could be affected by the decision, recused himself from the case last week and did not participate in the oral arguments.

That means only one Republican-appointed justice will need to vote with the three Democrat-appointed justices, who are likely to take Boulder’s side, in order for the case to be allowed to move forward in state court.

Justices Sonia Sotomayor and Ketanji Brown Jackson, both on the liberal wing of the court, signaled they wanted to see the case move forward in state court and questioned whether asking for a Supreme Court ruling was premature.

The Boulder case has not yet gone to trial and there hasn’t been a ruling on the underlying case. Jackson asked why the court shouldn’t wait to hear the case once the state court was finished with its considerations.

“When we think about the court's determinations about which cases it should hear, I wonder whether we should be considering matters like this essentially piecemeal,” Jackson said.

Kannon Shanmugam, an attorney representing Suncor Energy, argued that the case “involves an unprecedented effort to use state law to regulate global conduct.”

Municipalities, he said, would have the ability to “make national and international energy policy” if cases like Boulder’s were allowed to move forward.

Shanmugam said fossil fuel companies are now facing roughly three dozen lawsuits with more being filed “by the week,” and argued that the amount of money at stake for the companies adds urgency to the Supreme Court’s decision.

“We need an answer to this question sooner rather than later,” he said.

Kevin Russell, the attorney representing the city and county of Boulder, argued that states have always had the power to address injuries that happen within their borders, even if the root of those injuries exist out of state.

There’s nothing in the Constitution, Russell argued, that prevents lawsuits at the state level even if the harm was widespread, the damages could be large, or the defendants are part of an important industry.

And, he contended, Boulder’s lawsuit was not aiming to prohibit fossil fuel companies from doing business. “It requires them to internalize a portion of the cost of their activities by paying for some of the damage that those activities inflict,” he said.

entries.title: Barack Obama to Campaign With Abdul El-Sayed in Detroit
entries.summary: The former president has been stepping up his involvement in this year’s midterm elections.
entries.content:
Former President Barack Obama will campaign with Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in Detroit later this month, the Michigan Senate hopeful announced on Monday.

“It is my honor and privilege to announce that President @BarackObama is joining us on the trail in Detroit on Saturday, October 24,” El-Sayed wrote Monday on X. “Get. Ready.”

The rally will also feature Democratic gubernatorial nominee Jocelyn Benson, and falls on the first day of Michigan’s mandatory early in-person voting period.

El-Sayed is facing Republican Mike Rogers for the open seat held by retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters — a tight race that polling has shown is neck-and-neck.

Detroit is also an important target for El-Sayed. He lost Wayne County, home to the state’s largest city, to Rep. Haley Stevens in the Democratic primary, despite narrowly winning statewide. Former Vice President Kamala Harris campaigned with him in Detroit last month.

Obama has been stepping up his involvement in the midterms. He taped two dozen ads last week for Democratic Senate and gubernatorial candidates, with more campaign stops planned in the final weeks before the election, according to the Associated Press.

entries.title: LGBTQ+ Group Turns Its Back on Democrats Adopting GOP Trans Rhetoric
entries.summary: “I'm not wasting my time on Marcy Kaptur,” said Human Rights Campaign President Kelley Robinson.
entries.content:
Some national LGBTQ+ groups are turning their backs on Democrats who have adopted anti-transgender rhetoric in their campaigns this election cycle.

“You don't have to sacrifice any member of our community to win in these races to have a message that resonates with voters,” Kelley Robinson, president of the Human Rights Campaign, said in a briefing for reporters Monday morning.

After failing to respond to President Donald Trump’s anti-transgender ads in the 2024 presidential election, some Democrats have been addressing the issue by borrowing Republicans’ terminology, often opposing trans athletes’ participation in women’s sports. According to a September poll from The 19th and YouGov, 45% of adults say they are more likely to vote for candidates who support trans athlete bans, compared with 20% who say they’d back someone who opposes them.

In Ohio, the Democratic gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton told The Toledo Blade, “I do not support boys in girls’ sports.” Rep. Marcy Kaptur (D-Ohio) released an ad in which she says “boys should not play in girls’ sports.”

Those two candidates, Robinson said, will not receive the Human Rights Campaign’s support ahead of November.

“You've got Marcy Kaptur, who not only is bad on the message, but she's also bad on the policy,” Robinson said, referring to how Kaptur voted in support of a bill that would have required schools to ask for parental consent before allowing trans students from using their preferred pronouns and names.

“We're spending our energy investing in the candidates that are all the way with us. So in Ohio, we're really spending a lot of energy and effort with Sherrod Brown's [Senate] campaign. We're not supporting Amy Acton or Marcy Kaptur at this time,” Robinson added. “If these folks are elected, we'll figure out how to operate on the other side.”

Robinson said that Brown, who is running against Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio), has done a “great job” responding to Republicans’ anti-trans attacks.

An Human Rights Campaign survey of over 9,000 LGBTQ+ adults that the group released at the briefing found respondents “have little confidence in major political and public institutions,” and nearly 40% said they had “very little” confidence in the Democratic Party. At the same time, nearly nine in 10 said they plan to vote in November.

A 30-second ad from Brown’s campaign has voters, not Brown, explicitly saying that anti-trans messaging in the state is a distraction from economic issues because Ohio already has laws in place banning gender-affirming care for minors and prohibiting trans athletes from joining female sports teams.

“I'm not wasting my time on Marcy Kaptur,” Robinson said. “We're spending our energy and resources on the champions that we think can be the difference makers.”

The organization has had conversations with some Democratic candidates that have made anti-trans remarks.

Texas Senate Democratic candidate James Talarico told Fox News that he opposed “trans athletes playing in girls’ sports if it endangers safety or fairness,” and he would “absolutely” vote for a bill to ban gender-affirming surgeries for minors. Robinson said that Talarico, who the Human Rights Campaign has endorsed, apologized at a campaign event in Houston two days later.

She said he explained that his comments got clipped so his overall approach to the issue wasn’t clear, and that he believed in most cases that there are no safety or fairness issues when trans kids play sports.

“That was a caveat that he put in there, really encouraging folks to go back to local governance and rules related to sports and he felt like that wasn’t really captured,” Robinson said.

She added that Talarico clarified his position on gender-affirming care, saying “he believed that the role of politicians isn’t in the doctor’s office.”

The campaigns of Acton, Kaptur and Talarico did not respond to The Washington Sun’s requests for comment.

In April, the Human Rights Campaign announced that it planned to spend $15 million this cycle in voter outreach efforts in key races. Robinson said her group does “not endorse every Democrat,” and that the investment would be going to “folks who are with us on the issues.”

entries.title: A Murder in Okinawa Tests U.S.-Japan Relationship
entries.summary: U.S. government and military officials received summons from Japanese leaders after local police arrested a Marine in connection with a woman’s murder.
entries.content:
A U.S. Marine's arrest on suspicion of murder in Okinawa, Japan, over the weekend has inflamed tensions between the two allies and raised new questions about the heavy U.S. military presence on the island.

Several U.S. government and military officials received protest letters and summons from Japanese leaders after local police arrested the 20-year-old Marine, Devin Jacob Ballard, on Saturday in connection with the killing of a local woman.

“The occurrence of such an extremely brutal and heinous incident is a matter of profound regret, and as the Government of Japan, we have lodged a strong protest with the U.S. side, while firmly demanding maximum cooperation with the investigation, strict discipline among U.S. military personnel, and thorough measures to prevent the recurrence of such incidents and accidents,” Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi wrote Sunday in a post on X.

The U.S. has maintained a continuous military presence in Japan since 1945, when American forces occupied Japan to enforce the country’s surrender and demilitarization at the end of World War II. Japanese leaders have supported strengthening the U.S. military presence in the country in recent years to bolster the country’s force posture to regional threats from China and North Korea.

But more than 70% of the land operated by U.S. military facilities in Japan is concentrated in Okinawa, which has led to increased tensions with locals.

Okinawa, part of a chain of Japanese islands situated close to China, hosts 32 U.S. military bases.

Japan’s Foreign Affairs Minister Toshimitsu Motegi summoned George Glass, the U.S. ambassador to Japan, in a rare formal complaint on Sunday following the arrest of the Marine.

“Ambassador Glass reiterated deep regret over the loss of life and reaffirmed that the U.S. side will cooperate fully with Japanese authorities in their investigations, and the U.S. side is committed to doing everything they can to prevent such incidents,” the Ministry said in a news release.

Glass said in a post on X Monday that he had assured Japanese officials, including Motegi and Okinawa Governor Genta Koja, that he plans to speak with U.S. military commanders this week about their efforts to “hold our American servicemembers to the very highest levels of discipline and integrity.”

Glass also spoke with Lt. Gen. Benjamin T. Watson, the commanding general of the Marine forces stationed in Japan, to address the U.S.’s “next steps in strengthening that bond of trust with our Japanese partners and base-hosting communities.”

Watson addressed reporters after Koja and Naha Mayor Satoru Chinen gave him a letter at the Okinawa prefectural office demanding a review of U.S.-Japan status of forces agreement and stricter discipline measures for U.S. personnel stationed in the country, according to Stars and Stripes.

“I meant it when I said that Okinawa is our home. It is my home, and any serious incidents that cause anxiety and concern for the people of Okinawa cause us concern,” Watson said Monday.

Okinawa prefectural police arrested Ballard, a 20-year-old Marine stationed at Futenma Air Station, on suspicion of strangling 39-year-old Anna Yagi. Ballard is accused of killing Yagi at a hotel in Naha, Okinawa’s capital city, early Saturday and stealing her personal belongings, according to The Associated Press.

Several Japanese media outlets reported that Ballard denied the allegation and told investigators, “I don't know anything about it.”

Japanese citizens also launched protests over the weekend to the large U.S. military presence in their country, with more than 50,000 troops across all military branches stationed there, according to U.S. Forces Japan.

The alleged murder has reignited long-standing friction between the U.S. and Japan over criminal activity committed by American military personnel. Between 1972 and 2023, 6,124 people were arrested for criminal offenses committed by U.S. military personnel, and 759 were arrested for crimes such as murder, robbery and sexual assault, according to a 2024 police report cited by the Okinawan newspaper Ryukyu Shimpo.

entries.title: Politico Was Barred From Traveling With Trump on Air Force One
entries.summary: The outlet was supposed to fly with the president as the print pool representative.
entries.content:
The White House refused to allow Politico to travel with President Donald Trump aboard Air Force One on Monday, a spokesperson for the outlet said.

Politico is part of a trio of news companies, along with CNN and MS NOW, that Trump banned from the White House on Sept. 18, and several journalists had their media passes confiscated when they tried to enter the grounds. Judge Timothy J. Kelly issued a temporary restraining order on the policy on Sept. 24 and directed the White House to reinstate the journalists’ passes.

Politico confirmed that the outlet had been excluded from the out-of-town travel pool on Monday, despite Kelly’s order. The outlet was slated to be the print pool representative on Monday. CNN first reported the news.

CNN had also been blocked from fulfilling its pool duties on the days the network was assigned to be the TV pool representative.

Trump is set to travel to Nebraska for a campaign stop in Grand Island.

The White House defended its decision in a statement to The Washington Sun, saying that “Trump is the most accessible President in American history” because of the frequency with which he appears in front of reporters and the fact that he posts often on social media.

“Many outlets including Politico are granted access to attend and cover presidential events unilaterally, but traveling with the President of the United States aboard Air Force One is a privilege not a right,” a White House spokesperson added.

White House Communications Director Steven Cheung previously said he believes that Kelly’s order restoring access to the White House grounds does not cover journalists’ ability to cover the president through pool events.

“The judge basically ordered them to renew their access back to the White House, but that’s different than allowing the pool into the events in the Oval Office or on Air Force One,” Cheung told TIME on Sept. 28 during the outlet’s interview with the president.

In his order, Kelly cited due process concerns spurred by the White House confiscating journalists’ badges without prior notice or an appropriate opportunity to be heard regarding the decision.

But Kelly’s order did not specify whether the White House can legally ban journalists conducting their pool duties, which are agreements in which a rotating group of journalists cover an event or political figure and share material and information with the wider press corps. Journalists covering Trump may have to execute their pool responsibilities within the White House grounds, or they can work through a travel pool if the president has a scheduled trip.

Kelly’s temporary restraining order expires Thursday. Attorneys for the media outlets filed a motion on Sept. 28 urging Kelly to issue a preliminary injunction to block the ban while the case proceeds in court. Kelly has not issued a ruling on the media outlet’s request, but a hearing is scheduled Thursday to review the motion.

“The White House has persisted in unpredictably and inconsistently implementing its ban, including by barring CNN from fulfilling its role as designated television network pooler on September 26—to the detriment of CNN, its fellow pool members and, ultimately, the American public,” the filing from media outlets reads.

This story has been updated with additional information.

entries.title: Rep. Beatty Asks a Judge to Compel Evidence in Kennedy Center Lawsuit
entries.summary: The Justice Department has asserted presidential privilege over requests involving Trump and White House officials.
entries.content:
Rep. Joyce Beatty is asking a federal judge to force the Justice Department to turn over documents about President Donald Trump’s role in the Kennedy Center’s planned two-year shutdown, accusing the administration of improperly shielding evidence behind presidential privilege.

In a motion filed Monday, Beatty’s attorneys said the administration has “stonewalled discovery” by withholding communications between Trump and Kennedy Center officials.

“Trump is the one running the show,” Beatty’s lawyers wrote, arguing that his role as chairman of the Kennedy Center’s board does not allow him to shield those communications.

The motion asks U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper to order the administration to turn over documents and answer questions about the closure.

Beatty, a Democrat from Ohio and an ex officio member of the Kennedy Center board, has challenged Trump’s efforts to reshape the institution since he took control of its board and leadership.

The administration says the Kennedy Center needs extensive renovations because of deteriorating infrastructure and safety problems. But Trump has repeatedly linked the project to his demand that his name be recognized on the building.

In a Time magazine interview published last week, Trump declined to rule out demolishing the Kennedy Center if his name isn’t added to the center.

“I’m not committing to anything,” Trump said when asked whether he would agree not to bring wrecking balls to the building without congressional approval.

Beatty’s attorneys cited those comments as evidence that discovery into Trump’s communications with Kennedy Center officials is critical.

The filing also points to Cooper’s earlier finding that the board’s initial decision to close the center was based on a “stacked deck” and “serious informational deficits.” The board voted again in August and September to shut down the building for two years.

Beatty’s attorneys say Trump was closely involved in the closure effort from the start. According to the filing, he announced the two-year shutdown before the board voted on it and later joked that the board’s approval was “a little late.”

Matt Floca, the executive director for the Kennedy Center, also has testified that he had “numerous conversations” with Trump, sometimes “multiple times a day,” about the building. Trump weighed in on details including seat colors and repainting the center’s historic columns, according to the filing.

The administration previously relied on communications between Trump and Floca when defending the closure, Beatty’s attorneys wrote. Her lawyers now argue the government cannot use those communications to support its case while blocking Beatty from obtaining more evidence about them.

The Justice Department has asserted presidential communications privilege over requests involving Trump and White House officials, including records held by the Kennedy Center, according to the motion.

The Justice Department didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Beatty’s lawyers argue that privilege does not apply because the Kennedy Center is not part of the executive branch and Trump was acting as the institution’s board chairman.

“Defendants cannot collectively excuse themselves from the discovery obligations that would otherwise apply to all Board members just because one of them also happens to be President,” the filing says.

The administration produced about 100 documents on Sept. 30, including roughly 35 emails, according to Monday’s motion. Beatty’s attorneys say the Justice Department has withheld information about how the closure could affect performers, programming, employees, audiences, donors and the Kennedy Center’s finances.

The dispute is the latest in Beatty’s legal battle over Trump’s control of the Kennedy Center.

In May, Cooper ordered Trump’s name removed from the building and blocked the planned two-year closure. The board later tried to put his name back on the building, prompting another legal challenge from Beatty.

The Kennedy Center has been closed since Sept. 15. Cooper has also ordered the center to give advance notice before making changes to its renovation plans, including potential demolition.

Beatty’s latest motion asks Cooper to compel the administration to produce the disputed records.

“Absent the Court’s intervention, Defendants will be allowed to curate the record and hide the truth from the Court,” her attorneys wrote.

entries.title: Trump Says He’ll Pay for Promotional Ads Instead of Taxpayers
entries.summary: The president added that he and his super PAC would cover the cost of the controversial pro-Trump ads.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump announced Monday that he will begin paying for the controversial slate of promotional ad spots — which had previously been funded by U.S. taxpayers — using his own money or funds raised by a pro-Trump super PAC.

“The Radical Left is upset with the fact that I am taking Ads, which I consider to be a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A., and paying for them with U.S.A. money,” Trump wrote on Truth Social on Monday. “I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc.”

Federal campaign-finance law makes it illegal for a U.S. president to direct the spending decisions of a super PAC. Trump has frequently called MAGA Inc. — the $400 million super PAC run by his political allies — “my money that I control.”

Last month, a campaign watchdog group submitted an official complaint with federal election regulators, arguing that Trump’s oversight of MAGA Inc. violates the law.

Lawmakers, including Senate Majority Leader John Thune, have criticized the White House’s recent ad spending as potentially illegal and a misuse of taxpayer funds after it siphoned $20 million in Homeland Security funds to bankroll the ads, including one earlier this week that was similar to a 2024 Trump campaign ad.

Trump has argued that the ads are legal because they don’t promote him directly, but instead promote the United States. He told reporters last week that he will “gladly” pay for the ads “if somebody said that that’s wrong.”

Trump did not say whether money already spent on ad spots would be reimbursed to taxpayers by the president or his PAC.

entries.title: Supreme Court Rejects Appeal Over School's Ban on ‘Let’s Go Brandon’ Sweatshirts
entries.summary: Lower courts found the prohibition on the veiled vulgarity didn't violate the First Amendment.
entries.content:
By Lindsay Whitehurst

The Supreme Court won't hear a challenge to a school district's ban on shirts with the phrase “Let’s Go Brandon.”

The phrase is a jab at former President Joe Biden with a coded reference to profanity. A Michigan mother of two says the school's ban is a First Amendment violation.

The school told her sons to take off the sweatshirts she bought them for Christmas in 2022.

Lower courts upheld the ban, finding the veiled vulgarity of the phrase allows schools to ban it. It functions as a stand-in for “F-— Joe Biden."

The woman's attorneys argued that the decision wrongly gives school officials wide latitude to squelch political speech based on their personal ideas of what is vulgar. The phrase itself doesn't contain any swear words or sexual implications, they said.

The school district urged the justices to reject the case, arguing that messages with lewd implications have no place in school, even if they touch on political topics. There has been evidence that some students wore clothing that read “Make America Great Again” or had messages supporting President Donald Trump, a Republican who lost the 2020 election to Biden, a Democrat.

The phrase originated in 2021, when people in the crowd at a NASCAR race chanted the obscenity directed at Biden and a TV sports reporter said they were calling out “Let’s Go, Brandon," apparently believing they were chanting for driver Brandon Brown, who had just won a race.
